question: Does sufficiently broad pretraining place large neural networks in weight-space neighborhoods where task-improving but task-specialized parameter perturbations are dense enough that one can replace iterative post-training with a single parallel draw, validation-set top-K selection, and prediction ensembling?

key_findings.claim: Under one fixed isotropic Gaussian probe, the fraction of perturbations that match or improve a task rises sharply with Qwen2.5-Instruct model scale.
key_findings.evidence: Solution density is defined as delta(m)=P_epsilon[s(theta+epsilon)>=s(theta)+m] for epsilon drawn from N(0,sigma^2 I), with sigma=0.005 in the landscape experiments. Figure 12 reports that the fraction of 500 perturbations matching or exceeding the base rises from 0% to 64% on GSM8K and from 8% to 60% on Countdown as scale grows from 0.5B to 32B; Figure 3 reports monotonic scaling for several positive margins m. This is compelling evidence for the sampled distribution, not a coordinate-free measure of surrounding volume.

key_findings.claim: The 'density of experts' is distribution-, parameterization-, noise-scale-, margin-, and evaluator-dependent, so the paper does not establish an intrinsic geometric density of the full weight neighborhood.
key_findings.evidence: The definition fixes raw-coordinate isotropic noise and the main landscape study fixes sigma=0.005; RandOpt later uses the discrete set {0.001,0.002,0.003}. No layer-wise normalization, reparameterization test, radius sweep for the scaling law, or functional-distance control is reported. In billions of dimensions, changing parameter units or sigma changes the Gaussian shell and therefore delta(m), while benchmark formatting changes s(theta). The operational statistic remains useful as a hit rate but should not be read as Lebesgue volume or a model-invariant landscape property.

key_findings.claim: Task rankings of random perturbations become less correlated with model scale, supporting specialization in benchmark behavior but not proving distinct mechanistic experts or nearby task minima.
key_findings.evidence: Across N=500 perturbations and M=7 tasks, Spectral Discordance is one minus the mean off-diagonal Pearson correlation of percentile-rank columns and rises monotonically across Qwen2.5 scales. Spiky rank profiles and a 2D PCA/K-means visualization show complementary task performance. Appendix H proves 0<=D<=M/(M-1), which is about 1.17 for M=7; D=1 means zero average correlation, while values above one reflect net anticorrelation. Average correlation can also hide a mixture of positive and negative task pairs, and no cluster-stability or functional mechanism test is supplied.

anchors.section: H Derivation of Spectral Discordance Bounds

key_findings.claim: A one-dimensional autoregressive toy problem reproduces needle, thicket, and plateau regimes and supplies the paper's clearest causal evidence that diverse pretraining can create useful local variation.
key_findings.evidence: An MLP next-value predictor is either untrained, pretrained on a mixture of sinusoidal, linear, harmonic, sigmoidal, sawtooth, and square-wave signals, or pretrained only on linear signals. With N=1000 perturbations, mixed pretraining and sigma=0.002 yields diverse continuations from which the top five fit a target; no pretraining requires sigma=0.05 merely to create visible variation and still misses good continuations; single-type pretraining is already at ceiling. Appendix Tables 5-6 add held-out functions and mean ensembling, but their plotted results do not isolate which aspect of LLM pretraining causes the analogous scaling.

anchors.section: 3 A Minimal Setting In Which Thickets Emerge
F Needle, Thicket, and Plateau Regimes

key_findings.claim: RandOpt is a one-round selection-and-ensemble procedure, not an optimization-free or data-free learner.
key_findings.evidence: The method draws N seeds and noise scales, evaluates every theta+sigma_i epsilon(seed_i) on a labeled post-training set, retains the top K scores, and majority-votes their test predictions. Main experiments use N=5000, K=50, scales {0.001,0.002,0.003}, and the first 200 training samples. It has no gradient or sequential parameter update, but it performs N times D task evaluations, selects on supervised reward, stores or regenerates K weight perturbations, and ordinarily pays K forward passes per test example.

anchors.section: E Implementation Details / E.2 Method-Specific Compute

key_findings.claim: Across the full seven-task table, RandOpt reliably improves many base models and is often competitive with single-pass post-training baselines, but it is not uniformly best and frequently loses to an ensembled ES baseline.
key_findings.evidence: For Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, base versus RandOpt is 10.0 versus 58.4 on Countdown, 79.8 versus 87.1 on GSM8K, 58.6 versus 68.7 on MATH-500, and 24.5 versus 39.2 on OlympiadBench. Yet ES+TT-MV scores 61.9, 87.9, 67.7, and 39.7 on those tasks; ES also beats RandOpt on MBPP (77.2 versus 75.9), ROCStories (64.5 versus 56.5), and USPTO (52.9 versus 42.3). On Qwen-0.5B, RandOpt Countdown 8.4 trails PPO 14.8, GRPO 13.0, ES 14.9, and ES+TT-MV 11.2. The result supports competitiveness conditioned on training and inference budget definitions, not broad dominance.

anchors.section: D Full Results on LLM / Figure 11
Table 4 Experimental Results on Reasoning Benchmarks

key_findings.claim: The strongest headline comparisons equalize estimated training FLOPs but not inference compute, and the paper itself shows that test-time ensembling explains a large part of the apparent method gap.
key_findings.evidence: RandOpt and ES+TT-MV use K=50 test-time predictions, whereas PPO and GRPO are plotted with one pass; Figure 6 explicitly says this disadvantages those baselines but reflects standard usage. Figure 1(c) reports that 50-pass majority vote lifts PPO, GRPO, and ES toward roughly 79%, and Table 4 shows Qwen-0.5B ES increasing from 42.6% to 61.2% GSM8K when TT-MV is added. RandOpt K=1 is substantially weaker than K=50. Therefore equal training FLOPs do not isolate the value of random weight selection from the value and cost of ensembling.

anchors.section: Figure 6 / 5.4 Can Ensembling Also Benefit the Baselines?
5.4 Can Ensembling Also Benefit the Baselines?

key_findings.claim: One appendix statement assigns a baseline's 61.2% result to RandOpt, creating a concrete internal numerical contradiction.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix G says that on Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, 'RandOpt improves GSM8k performance from 39.9% (Base) to 61.2%.' Table 4 instead reports Base 39.9%, RandOpt 54.1%, and ES+TT-MV 61.2%; Section 5.4 also explicitly attributes the 42.6-to-61.2 increase to ES plus test-time majority vote. The 54.1% table value should be treated as the RandOpt result unless corrected by the authors.

anchors.section: 5.4 Can Ensembling Also Benefit the Baselines?

key_findings.claim: The VLM result is large but rests on one model-benchmark pair and retains the same 50-pass ensemble cost.
key_findings.evidence: Perturbing only the language model of Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct while freezing the visual encoder, with N=5000 and K=50, raises GQA accuracy from 56.6% to 69.0%, a 12.4-point gain. No other VLM, visual task, single-perturbation result, or equal-inference baseline is reported, so it is a proof of cross-modality rather than a broad VLM scaling result.

key_findings.claim: Population, selection-ratio, and model-scale sweeps reveal a finite regime of usefulness rather than an unlimited random-search scaling law.
key_findings.evidence: On Countdown with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, performance rises approximately log-linearly with N at sufficiently low K/N and the optimal selection ratio decreases as N grows. RandOpt fails near zero from scratch, offers little at GPT-2 0.1B and Qwen 0.5B, rises sharply around 1.5B, and then its relative advantage shrinks as the base approaches a plateau. The paper and Appendix D note saturation in both N and model size and warn that the exact curves may be task/model specific.

anchors.section: 11 Limitations / Capacity to Learn Dramatically New Skills?
D Population Scaling and Selection Ratio Saturation

key_findings.claim: The appendix's population-scaling labels and one-step budget are internally inconsistent, so the reported 87.1% one-step comparison cannot be assigned an unambiguous RandOpt population from Figure 13 alone.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 10 plots Population Size N and Selection Ratio K/N, with legends for K/N and N, but its caption reverses the symbols by calling them population size K and ensemble size N. On page 20, the Figure 13 prose says RandOpt (N=3000) reaches 87.1%, while the caption says N=5000,K=50; Table 4 and Appendix E define the main 87.1% GSM8K run as N=5000,K=50. The plotted star is near 3000 on the logarithmic x-axis, so the prose and figure geometry agree with N=3000, whereas the caption and reused main-table result agree with N=5000. This does not negate the comparison to the displayed one-step PPO/GRPO points, but it prevents exact reproduction and leaves unclear whether the identical 87.1% was remeasured at N=3000 or copied from the N=5000 run.

anchors.section: D Scaling Parallelism of the Baselines / Figure 13 prose and caption

key_findings.claim: RandOpt has constant sequential update depth only under massive parallelism; its measured wall-clock result does not establish a compute or hardware-efficiency advantage over matched baselines.
key_findings.evidence: A deployment on 200 GH200 GPUs samples N=2000, ensembles K=50, and reaches 70% Countdown accuracy for OLMo-3-7B-Instruct in 3.2 minutes. The O(1) claim counts training rounds, while total evaluation work remains proportional to N times the selection set and model size. No PPO/GRPO/ES run on the same 200-GPU allocation and wall-clock protocol is shown, and the simplified FLOP equations omit communication, reward evaluation, variable generated lengths, memory, and 50-pass inference.

anchors.section: E.1 FLOPs Calculation / E.2 Method-Specific Compute

key_findings.claim: Distillation recovers most, but not all, of the top-50 ensemble gain while abandoning RandOpt's no-update and fully parallel properties.
key_findings.evidence: The top 50 models generate 25,000 responses on 500 GSM8K training examples; hard examples are used for two SFT epochs. Qwen2.5-1.5B moves from 58.8 base to 74.9 distilled versus 76.4 RandOpt, and Qwen2.5-3B moves from 79.8 to 84.3 versus 87.1. The paper estimates distillation at about 2% of the original N=5000 selection cost, but it requires gradient training, reasoning traces, task-specific hard-example selection, and a categorical final answer.

key_findings.claim: A large fraction of measured GSM8K gain is format correction, and the residual 'reasoning thicket' category is an outcome decomposition rather than evidence of a distinct reasoning mechanism.
key_findings.evidence: For Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct with N=3000 and K=50, RandOpt reaches 86.7% overall, with 19.0% of examples credited to fixing strict output format, 12.3% to base-wrong/adapted-correct answers, and 0.7% regression. The second category shows corrected numerical outcomes, but it does not rule out altered sampling, parser behavior, memorized templates, or shallow heuristics; calling it a reasoning thicket is therefore operational. The paper appropriately concedes that 'expert' means doing well on the benchmark and can mix format, personality, knowledge, and skill.

key_findings.claim: The diffusion-model 'color thicket' extension remains qualitative and does not yet validate density, diversity, or competitive adaptation outside discrete-answer tasks.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix J perturbs Stable Diffusion XL, uses GPT-5.2 to select top-K models for target words such as 'blue' or 'yellow', and mean-ensembles model predictions at each denoising step. Tables 7-8 show training- and held-out-prompt image grids but no quantitative color score, population/ensemble ablation, baseline, uncertainty, or cost. It illustrates a possible structured-output aggregation rule, not evidence comparable to the LLM tables.

method.core_idea: Treat a pretrained parameter vector as the center of a task-conditioned sampling distribution: measure how often small Gaussian perturbations improve each task, select the best perturbations on a small task dataset, and exploit their complementary errors by majority-vote ensembling rather than iteratively updating one model.
method.mechanism: For landscape analysis, draw raw-parameter perturbations epsilon from N(0,sigma^2 I), compute each task score and the hit probability above a margin, and compare cross-task percentile rankings with Spectral Discordance. RandOpt samples N seeds and one scale per seed from a small set, evaluates each perturbed model theta_i=theta+sigma_i epsilon(seed_i) on the first 200 training examples, retains the top K, and majority-votes their generated answers at inference. The implementation compares N=5000,K=50 one-round selection against equal-estimated-training-FLOP PPO, GRPO, and iterative ES; an optional SFT stage distills ensemble-produced reasoning traces into one model.
assumptions: Raw-coordinate isotropic Gaussian noise with a shared global sigma defines a meaningful and comparable local neighborhood across layers, model families, sizes, and parameterizations.
The chosen sigma values are small enough to probe one pretrained basin but large enough to expose useful functional diversity.
A benchmark score on the first 200 training examples reliably selects perturbations that generalize to the test set rather than overfit formatting or sample idiosyncrasies.
Strict answer extractors and rewards measure the intended skill; format adherence is not conflated with reasoning unless explicitly decomposed.
Low cross-task rank correlation indicates useful task specialists rather than measurement noise, reward hacking, or accidental parser differences.
Task-wise performance vectors and their average Pearson correlations adequately summarize diversity; pairwise signs and nonlinear dependence need not be modeled.
Majority voting is defined and beneficial because most main tasks reduce outputs to a discrete answer or label.
Top-K errors are sufficiently independent that ensemble accuracy transfers from the selection set to held-out examples.

Estimated forward/backward FLOP formulas at fixed maximum length adequately equalize training budgets despite variable generation length, reward computation, reference/critic models, memory, and communication.
Inference-time compute can be treated separately from training compute even though RandOpt's main results use K=50 passes and PPO/GRPO usually use one.
Enough parallel accelerators are available to turn N independent evaluations into constant sequential depth; O(1) rounds is meaningful to the deployment setting.
Model-size trends are not driven primarily by different absolute base accuracies, tokenizers, calibration, or a fixed sigma interacting differently with parameter scale.
Base-wrong/adapted-correct GSM8K answers reflect reasoning improvement even without a causal or mechanistic analysis of the generated trace.

techniques.role: Defines solution density as the probability that a sampled raw-weight perturbation exceeds the base task score by margin m.
Measures specialization as one minus the mean cross-task correlation of perturbation percentile ranks.
Creates a controlled toy model in which pretraining diversity can be varied to produce needle, thicket, and plateau regimes.
Represents each candidate with a random seed and scalar noise level instead of storing a separately trained checkpoint.
Evaluates an independently sampled population once and retains the K best validation-scoring perturbations.
Aggregates categorical predictions from selected parameter perturbations to exploit complementary task behavior.
Budgets PPO, GRPO, ES, and RandOpt using simplified per-token forward/backward FLOP accounting.
Separates retained correctness, newly correct values, parser-format fixes, and regressions on GSM8K.
Turns top-50 reasoning traces into an SFT dataset so a single model recovers most ensemble performance.
Provides a proof-of-concept aggregation rule for structured diffusion outputs when majority vote is unavailable.

evaluations.setting: Qwen2.5-Instruct from 0.5B to 32B, 500-1000 full-parameter perturbations, sigma=0.005, on GSM8K, Countdown, and positive accuracy margins.
evaluations.metric: Solution density delta(m) and distribution of relative accuracy change.
evaluations.result: The fraction matching or exceeding base performance rises 0% to 64% on GSM8K and 8% to 60% on Countdown from 0.5B to 32B; reported density also increases monotonically for several positive margins.
evaluations.baseline: The unperturbed model at each scale and smaller pretrained models sampled with the same nominal sigma.

evaluations.setting: Five Qwen2.5 model scales, 500 perturbations each, evaluated on Countdown, GSM8K, MATH-500, OlympiadBench, MBPP, ROCStories, and USPTO.
evaluations.metric: Spectral Discordance, task-wise percentile spectra, PCA, and K-means organization of seven-dimensional performance vectors.
evaluations.result: Discordance rises monotonically with model size; individual spectra are spiky and the 2D projection shows clusters with different task strengths. Exact discordance values and cluster-stability statistics are not tabulated in extracted text.
evaluations.baseline: The generalist hypothesis in which all task rankings are positively aligned and D approaches zero.

evaluations.setting: Autoregressive MLP on random 1D signal families; no pretraining, mixed-family pretraining, or single-family pretraining; N=1000.
evaluations.metric: Qualitative rollout fit and appendix held-out-function mean squared error.
evaluations.result: Untrained models need sigma=0.05 to vary and still miss good continuations; mixed pretraining at sigma=0.002 yields selectable task-specific continuations and held-out improvement; matched single-family pretraining is already at a plateau.
evaluations.baseline: Xavier and Kaiming random initialization, the unperturbed mixed model, and a single-function-family pretrained model.

evaluations.setting: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct on seven tasks; RandOpt N=5000,K=50; all post-training methods matched on estimated training FLOPs, with ES+TT-MV also using 50 inference passes.
evaluations.metric: Test accuracy averaged over three runs.
evaluations.result: RandOpt scores 58.4+/-0.2 Countdown, 87.1+/-0.8 GSM8K, 68.7+/-0.7 MATH-500, 39.2+/-0.6 OlympiadBench, 75.9+/-0.6 MBPP, 56.5+/-0.3 ROCStories, and 42.3+/-0.3 USPTO, versus base 10.0/79.8/58.6/24.5/69.5/54.7/38.5. ES+TT-MV is higher on Countdown, GSM8K, and OlympiadBench; plain ES is higher on MBPP, ROCStories, and USPTO.
evaluations.baseline: Base, test-time majority vote, best-of-50, PPO, GRPO, iterative ES, and ES plus 50-pass majority vote.

evaluations.setting: OLMo3-7B-Instruct and transparent OLMo3-7B-Base across the same seven tasks.
evaluations.metric: Three-run test accuracy under equal estimated training FLOPs.
evaluations.result: On instruct, RandOpt reaches 85.0 Countdown and 73.7 MATH-500 versus base 64.8 and 60.6, but ES+TT-MV is higher on OlympiadBench (44.7 versus 35.4) and GRPO is higher on USPTO (51.0 versus 43.0). On base, RandOpt improves Countdown 9.8 to 30.2 and GSM8K 78.5 to 85.0, while ES+TT-MV wins MATH-500 69.0, OlympiadBench 43.3, and ROCStories 76.3.
evaluations.baseline: The corresponding base checkpoint, PPO, GRPO, ES, test-time majority vote, best-of-50, and ES plus majority vote.

evaluations.setting: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct GSM8K, one training step, grid-searching PPO batch size 128-2048 and GRPO group size 512-8192. RandOpt's population is internally inconsistent: N=3000 in the prose and plotted star, but N=5000,K=50 in the Figure 13 caption.
evaluations.metric: Accuracy versus one-step parallel batch or population size.
evaluations.result: Best PPO reaches 78.0%, best GRPO 83.5%, and RandOpt 87.1%; simply enlarging PPO/GRPO batch/group size does not monotonically close the displayed one-round gap. Exact replication requires resolving whether RandOpt used N=3000 or N=5000 and whether 87.1% was independently measured or reused from Table 4.
evaluations.baseline: One-step PPO and GRPO at learning rates 1e-5, 1e-6, and 1e-7.

evaluations.setting: Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct on GQA, perturbing the language model only, with N=5000 and K=50.
evaluations.result: Accuracy increases from 56.6% to 69.0%, a 12.4-point absolute gain.
evaluations.baseline: The unperturbed Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct model; no equal-inference adaptation baseline is reported.

evaluations.setting: Countdown with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, sweeping population N and selection ratio K/N; separate model-scale sweep including from-scratch and pretrained checkpoints.
evaluations.metric: Accuracy versus log population, K/N, and parameter count.
evaluations.result: Accuracy rises approximately log-linearly with N at low selection ratios, optimal K/N decreases with N, from-scratch performance stays near zero, gains emerge around 1.5B, and relative improvement later saturates.
evaluations.baseline: The base checkpoint at each size and RandOpt applied to untrained weights.

evaluations.setting: OLMo-3-7B-Instruct Countdown on a 200-GH200 cluster, N=2000,K=50.
evaluations.result: The run takes 3.2 minutes and reaches 70% accuracy; no baseline is timed on the identical hardware allocation.
evaluations.baseline: The conceptual O(T)-round PPO, GRPO, and ES alternatives rather than an empirically matched wall-clock run.

evaluations.setting: GSM8K ensemble distillation for Qwen2.5-1.5B- and 3B-Instruct; top 50 produce 25,000 responses on 500 examples, followed by hard-example SFT.
evaluations.metric: Single-model test accuracy and estimated distillation cost.
evaluations.result: For 1.5B, base/distilled/RandOpt are 58.8/74.9/76.4%; for 3B they are 79.8/84.3/87.1%. The paper estimates distillation at about 2% of the N=5000 selection compute.
evaluations.baseline: The base single model and the undistilled top-50 RandOpt ensemble.

evaluations.setting: All 1,319 GSM8K test examples with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, RandOpt N=3000,K=50.
evaluations.metric: Accuracy decomposed into retained correct, base-wrong/adapted-correct, format-fixed, and regression categories.
evaluations.result: Overall accuracy is 86.7%; 19.0% of examples are credited to format fixes, 12.3% to newly correct numerical answers, and 0.7% are regressions.
evaluations.baseline: The base model and GRPO under the same outcome-category analysis.

evaluations.setting: Stable Diffusion XL prompts with target words 'blue' or 'yellow'; GPT-5.2 selection; mean ensembling at each denoising step; separate held-out prompts.
evaluations.metric: Qualitative target-color adherence and transfer from train to test prompt grids.
evaluations.result: Selected ensembles visibly shift both training and held-out generations toward the target palette, but no numerical metric, baseline, variance, N/K sensitivity, or runtime is reported.
evaluations.baseline: Unquantified base generation; the appendix does not show other color-control or post-training algorithms.

limitations: Author-stated: RandOpt fails from scratch and struggles on small pretrained models because useful local solutions are too sparse.
Author-stated: gains saturate with both model size and log population, and the method may not acquire dramatically new skills outside the local neighborhood.
Author-stated: strong performance typically needs K>1 forward passes at inference; distillation adds sequential gradient training and is task-specific.
Author-stated: majority vote does not naturally support stories, images, molecules, or other structured outputs; diffusion mean ensembling is only a proof of concept.
Author-stated: the work characterizes but does not explain exactly when or why pretraining enters the thicket regime.
Reviewer-identified: solution density uses one raw-coordinate Gaussian and is not invariant to reparameterization, layer scale, sigma, or benchmark evaluator.
Reviewer-identified: equalized training-FLOP comparisons leave RandOpt and ES+TT-MV with 50 inference passes versus one for PPO/GRPO, so algorithm and ensemble benefits are confounded.
Reviewer-identified: the FLOP model assumes fixed sequence length and omits reward computation, communication, memory traffic, generation-length variation, and deployment inference cost.
Reviewer-identified: first-200-example top-K selection can overfit task format or validation idiosyncrasies; no selection-set-size or repeated-split study is reported.
Reviewer-identified: Spectral Discordance and K-means show benchmark-output diversity, not that perturbations are distinct mechanistic experts or local minima.
Reviewer-identified: only one VLM benchmark is tested, and the structured-output diffusion extension is qualitative.
Reviewer-identified: the 200-GPU 3.2-minute result has no same-hardware baseline and assumes unusually abundant parallel accelerators.
Reviewer-identified: Appendix G incorrectly attributes a 61.2% GSM8K value to RandOpt; Table 4 reports 54.1% for RandOpt and 61.2% for ES+TT-MV.

Reviewer-identified: Figure 10 reverses the meanings of N and K in its caption, while Figure 13 conflicts between N=3000 in prose/plot and N=5000,K=50 in its caption; the identical 87.1% main-table value makes the one-step RandOpt budget ambiguous.
Reviewer-identified: 19.0% of the showcased GSM8K gain is format correction, and the remaining outcome categories do not by themselves establish novel reasoning mechanisms.
failure_modes: A fixed sigma can be too small to change small or undertrained models, too large for sensitive layers, or incomparable across parameterizations.
Random perturbations from scratch or around weak representations remain in the needle regime and yield near-zero useful hit rates.
A model already near task ceiling enters the plateau regime, leaving no improvement for selection and making relative density misleading.
Selecting top K on only 200 examples can capture prompt format, answer-parser quirks, or spurious correlations that fail on the test distribution.
When task experts make correlated mistakes or K is too large, majority voting dilutes the rare best specialist with mediocre perturbations.
When K is too small, the method loses the ensemble effect that drives much of its reported competitiveness.
Continuous or structured predictions lack a canonical majority vote; naive mean ensembling can blur signals or generate invalid outputs.
Massive one-round populations can exceed device, communication, checkpoint-regeneration, or evaluation-bandwidth limits despite low sequential depth.
Benchmark rewards that heavily depend on tags or exact serialization create format thickets that look like skill acquisition.
Task correlations averaged into one discordance scalar can cancel and falsely imply orthogonality; noisy percentile ties can further distort ranks.
Distillation can lose minority specialist behavior, require unavailable reasoning traces, or reintroduce ordinary SFT overfitting.
Local random selection saturates when the target capability is absent from the pretrained representation, requiring directed updates or a larger search radius.
A mislabeled population or ensemble size can make a one-step compute comparison appear reproducible while silently changing total selection evaluations or inference cost.
reusable_insights: Before designing a sophisticated optimizer, measure the empirical hit rate of simple perturbations around the pretrained point at several radii and margins.
Decompose a multi-task pretrained objective into task-specific landscapes; aggregate flatness can hide nearby directions that trade one task against another.
Measure both density and diversity: a high hit rate is most exploitable when selected candidates make complementary errors.
Report parameter-noise normalization and functional distance, because raw-coordinate Gaussian density is otherwise not comparable across models.
Separate search compute, sequential depth, hardware parallelism, communication, and inference passes instead of calling all of them efficiency.
Give every baseline the same test-time ensemble budget when claiming the selection method, rather than ensembling alone, provides the gain.
Audit benchmark improvements for formatting, parser compliance, and reward shortcuts before interpreting them as new reasoning.
Use a mixed-pretraining toy model plus no-pretraining and task-matched ceiling controls to distinguish needle, adaptable, and plateau regimes.
Store perturbations as seed-scale pairs when reproducibility permits, avoiding K full checkpoint copies.
Distill a costly perturbation ensemble only after quantifying what diversity or minority expertise is lost in the single student.
For structured outputs, design a task-valid aggregation operator and evaluate it quantitatively rather than assuming categorical majority vote generalizes.
open_questions: Do density and discordance scaling persist under layer-normalized, Fisher-scaled, low-rank, or functionally matched perturbations?
How sensitive are the claimed phase transition near 1.5B and the 0.5B-to-32B hit rates to sigma, margin, tokenizer, and base accuracy?
Can a held-out validation protocol with repeated selection splits distinguish true local expertise from format and sample overfitting?
What mechanistic features or low-curvature subspaces make one perturbation improve a specific task while hurting another?
Does pretraining-task diversity causally produce LLM thickets, as in the 1D toy model, when data diversity and total compute are independently controlled?
How much of RandOpt's advantage remains after PPO, GRPO, ES, and the base model all receive identical K-pass inference compute?
Can adaptive but still one-round sampling allocate candidates across layers or scales more efficiently than a uniform discrete sigma mixture?
What is the sample complexity of top-K selection as a function of N, K, task variance, and the number of training examples?
Can one predict when local random search is incapable of acquiring a genuinely absent skill, rather than merely failing because N is too small?
Which ensemble operators preserve complementary expertise for code, free-form writing, molecule design, and image generation?
Can distillation retain specialist diversity through routing or mixture-of-experts instead of collapsing all top-K behavior into one model?
Do the OLMo and VLM results replicate with contamination-resistant tasks, larger base checkpoints, and independently implemented rewards?
What is the corrected Qwen2.5-0.5B GSM8K value intended by Appendix G, and do any claims change after resolving the 54.1/61.2 inconsistency?
Did the one-step Figure 13 RandOpt point use N=3000 or N=5000, and was its 87.1% independently rerun or copied from the main N=5000 Table 4 experiment?

competitive_landscape.title: Evolution Strategies at Scale: LLM Fine-Tuning Beyond Reinforcement Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest empirical competitor for full-parameter, Gaussian-perturbation, gradient-free LLM post-training at billion-parameter scale.
competitive_landscape.difference: Qiu et al. use many sequential ES generations to turn fitness-weighted perturbations into an updated single model and report advantages over RL. RandOpt spends a comparable evaluation budget on one independent population, selects top K without updating a center, and depends on inference ensembling; its contribution is parallel depth and specialist aggregation rather than a better learned parameter vector.

competitive_landscape.title: The Blessing of Dimensionality in LLM Fine-tuning: A Variance-Curvature Perspective
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct contemporary landscape explanation for why random weight perturbations and small-population ES can improve LLM rewards.
competitive_landscape.difference: Liang et al. attribute accessible improving directions to low-dimensional curvature embedded in a high-dimensional, degenerate reward landscape and analyze non-monotonic ES/GRPO dynamics. Neural Thickets instead measures task-conditioned hit rates and cross-task diversity, proposes one-round top-K ensembling, and offers a mixed-signal pretraining toy mechanism; it does not estimate curvature or identify the effective subspace.

competitive_landscape.title: PEP: Parameter Ensembling by Perturbation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Earlier direct method that treats pretrained weights as the center of a Gaussian parameter ensemble and requires no extra model training.
competitive_landscape.difference: PEP tunes one perturbation variance by validation ensemble likelihood and averages all perturbed classifiers to improve likelihood/calibration; it has no task-wise top-K candidate selection, model-scale density law, or multi-task specialization analysis. Its existence means Gaussian perturbation ensembling around trained weights is not new; RandOpt's narrower novelty is selective large-population use on LLM post-training and the thicket characterization.
competitive_landscape.source_version: NeurIPS 2020 official proceedings edition, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33, pages 8895-8906

competitive_landscape.title: Analyzing Reinforcement Learning Benchmarks with Random Weight Guessing
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct predecessor using distributions of independently guessed neural-network weights as a benchmark-complexity probe.
competitive_landscape.difference: Oller et al. sample small policy networks from scratch and analyze score distributions to expose easy RL benchmarks; they explicitly frame random guessing as analysis rather than a learning algorithm. Neural Thickets centers perturbations on pretrained billion-parameter models, studies scaling and cross-task specialization, and selects/ensembles top candidates as a practical post-training method.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv v1, submitted 16 April 2020; AAMAS 2020 paper

competitive_landscape.title: Fine-Tuning Language Models with Just Forward Passes
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct large-language-model competitor showing that full-parameter, forward-pass-only zeroth-order adaptation is practical after pretraining.
competitive_landscape.difference: MeZO performs many paired perturbation evaluations and applies an in-place zeroth-order SGD update to one model, emphasizing inference-level memory and learned task adaptation up to 66B parameters. RandOpt performs one independent population draw, never estimates or follows a gradient, and obtains its strongest results by selecting and ensembling K perturbed checkpoints. MeZO therefore predates the broad claim that forward-only post-training of large LMs is new, while RandOpt's narrower contribution is one-round specialist selection and the density/diversity probe.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv v3, revised 11 January 2024; NeurIPS 2023 oral version

competitive_landscape.title: Learning to Reason in 13 Parameters
competitive_landscape.relationship: Contemporary evidence that strong reasoning adaptations can lie in an extremely low-dimensional parameterization around a pretrained LLM.
competitive_landscape.difference: TinyLoRA trains as few as 13 shared adapter parameters with RL and reports 91% GSM8K for Qwen2.5-8B, directly supporting the idea that pretraining makes task-relevant weight changes highly accessible. It learns a single compact update rather than sampling isotropic full-parameter noise or ensembling experts, and its result concerns low trainable dimension rather than the probability mass or multi-task diversity of arbitrary nearby perturbations.

competitive_landscape.title: Spurious Rewards: Rethinking Training Signals in RLVR
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct empirical alternative explanation for why weak or uninformative post-training signals can improve selected pretrained models.
competitive_landscape.difference: Shao et al. show that GRPO with random or otherwise spurious rewards can amplify high-prior pretrained behaviors through clipping bias, with strong Qwen gains but failures on Llama3 and OLMo2. Neural Thickets instead samples raw weights without sequential policy updates and attributes success to local density and specialist diversity. The model-family dependence and concrete clipping mechanism caution against treating Qwen-local hit rates as a universal geometric phase transition.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims that large, well-pretrained models enter a previously uncharacterized 'thicket' regime in which diverse task experts occupy a substantial local fraction; that density and diversity scale with model size; and that RandOpt is the first practical fully parallel random-guess-and-check post-training method competitive with PPO, GRPO, and ES on contemporary LLMs and VLMs.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Qwen2.5 hit-rate and discordance curves, the mixed-signal causal toy model, seven-task Table 4 over Qwen/Llama/OLMo, one GQA result, population/model sweeps, a 200-GPU deployment, format decomposition, and distillation collectively substantiate the operational phenomenon. However, PEP already ensembles Gaussian perturbations around pretrained weights, Random Weight Guessing already treats score mass as a benchmark probe, ES at Scale and MeZO already demonstrate full-parameter forward-only LLM post-training, the Blessing of Dimensionality directly analyzes accessible improving perturbations, TinyLoRA finds reasoning updates in 13 learned parameters, and Spurious Rewards supplies a model-dependent behavioral/clipping account of weak-signal gains.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The strongest novelty is the joint empirical characterization of local task hit rate and cross-task rank discordance across LLM scale, plus using one-shot top-K validation selection and majority vote as an intentionally simple probe of that structure. Random parameter perturbation, weight-space score distributions, perturbation ensembling, forward-only LLM fine-tuning, and extremely low-dimensional reasoning adaptation are prior ideas. 'O(1)' is accurately a statement about sequential update rounds only under enough parallel hardware, and 'task expert' should remain an operational benchmark label because 19% of the highlighted GSM8K gain is formatting and no mechanistic specialist is identified. Claims of general competitive superiority should be narrowed to equal estimated training compute with usually unequal inference compute; Figure 13's unresolved N=3000/N=5000 conflict further prevents using that one-step panel as a precise budget-controlled estimate.

reviewer_notes: Secondary verification re-read the exact 30-page arXiv:2603.12228v1 artifact end to end, including references and Appendices A-J, all equations and prompts, the full seven-task Table 4, the graphical 1D-signal results, and the train/test diffusion grids. PDF metadata identifies v1; cached PDF/text hashes and all 30 extracted pages match the full-text index. The 0/10/37/64% GSM8K and 8/40/54/60% Countdown density sequences were visually checked in Figure 12, every quoted Table 4 cell was rechecked, and no graph-only MSE value was invented for Tables 5-6. The Appendix G 61.2% assignment is definitively inconsistent with RandOpt's 54.1% table cell, and the second pass newly recorded Figure 10's reversed N/K caption plus Figure 13's N=3000 prose/plot versus N=5000 caption ambiguity. Seven competitor identities, titles, mechanisms, and exact current primary versions were independently checked on 2026-08-23. Confidence is very high in transcription and internal-consistency findings, and deliberately lower in claims of intrinsic geometric density, mechanistic experts, and constant-time efficiency because those remain dependent on raw-coordinate noise, benchmark semantics, unequal inference accounting, and exceptional parallel hardware.
